item.title: Did the affordable care act keep patients out of the emergency department? Changes in Illinois, 2016-2024
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: A central premise of the Affordable Care Act was that broader coverage would mean fewer emergency department visits. A decade later, has that happened? To address the need for longer term evidence, we describe changes in Illinois ED visits between 2016, two years after ACA Medicaid expansion, and 2024, after pandemic fluctuations in visit rates.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of Illinois Hospital Association discharge data for ED visits in 2016 and 2024 by Illinois residents aged 18-64, the most insurance-sensitive age group. We analyzed visits by patient, hospital, and clinical characteristics, including ED visits for ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ACSC), as defined by the AHRQ Prevention Quality Indicators in ED Settings. Multivariable logistic regressions were used to estimate changes in the likelihood of an ACSC visit.

Results: Between 2016 and 2024, Illinois ED visits by residents aged 18-64 decreased from 3,168,399 to 2,653,154 (-16.3%). Visits identified as ACSC declined from 366,613 to 270,762, (-26.1%) with the largest decrease among the Medicaid-insured population. The odds of an ED visit for ACSC in 2024 compared to 2016 were lower for all patients (OR = 0.88 95% CI = 0.85-0.92). Decreases in odds were greatest for patients covered by Medicaid (17% lower) and Medicare disability (12% lower).

Conclusion: Declining ACSC visits, particularly among the Medicaid-insured, may reflect improved access to primary care. Insurance expansion is one part of the changing acute care delivery ecosystem, which includes increased telemedicine and urgent care centers as well as rising costs.

item.title: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection without chest pain identified on a triage electrocardiogram
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an uncommon but potentially devastating cause of myocardial infarction (MI) that may present without chest pain, making the diagnosis challenging. SCAD differs from atherosclerotic MI in both mechanism and risk profile: it predominantly affects women in midlife with few traditional cardiovascular risk factors, and is associated with fibromuscular dysplasia, recent emotional or physical stressors, and pregnancy. This report describes a 74-year-old woman who presented to the emergency department (ED) for a gastroenterology referral without chest pain and was found to have anterior ST elevations from a distal left anterior descending artery dissection. Although her age, atherosclerotic risk factors, and absence of chest pain were atypical, her sex and anterior ST changes were characteristic of SCAD, and a preceding period of physical stress may have contributed. A triage ECG led to catheterization before her troponin resulted.

item.title: Follow-up of human papillomavirus positive patients after self-collection in the emergency department
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Emergency department (ED) patients often lack sufficient primary care access and are disproportionately under-screened for cervical cancer compared with the general population. The recent FDA approval of self-collection for HPV testing at healthcare sites may facilitate cervical cancer screening for some patients. Thus, we investigated the proposition that the ED presents an opportunity to engage otherwise hard-to-reach individuals with cervical cancer screening via in-ED self-collection for HPV testing. While HPV negative individuals do not require further screening, HPV positive individuals require additional steps in the outpatient setting to complete screening.

Objective: After recent completion of a feasibility study of HPV self-collection among eligible ED patients in which more than 80% of participants agreed to self-collect and approximately 75% successfully completed self-collection in the ED, we followed the individuals who tested positive for HPV to assess their rate of follow-up for outpatient completion of screening.

Methods: We conducted follow-up at 150 days via electronic health record review and telephone survey to determine the follow-up rate for individuals who tested positive for HPV after in-ED self-collection.

Results: Among the individuals who successfully completed self-collection for HPV in the parent study, 24 (15.9%) tested positive for HPV. At 150 days, 7 (29.2%) out of 24 had completed screening (1 additional participant had scheduled upcoming screening). Individuals with higher triage acuity were less likely to follow up for additional screening.

Conclusion: Additional supports are required to maximize follow-up for completion of screening among those who test positive after in-ED self-collection for HPV testing.

item.title: Serum lactate distribution across neurologic emergencies: implications for seizure identification
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Serum lactate is routinely measured in emergency departments (EDs) as a marker of systemic metabolic stress, but its distribution across neurologic emergencies is poorly characterized. We evaluated serum lactate distributions among patients with suspected neurologic emergencies and its utility for seizure identification.

Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 22,430 consecutive ED visits and identified 637 ambulance-transported patients with suspected neurologic emergencies. All underwent venous blood gas analysis and non-contrast computed tomography on arrival. Serum lactate levels were compared among seizure (SZ), cerebral infarction (INF), transient ischemic attack (TIA), subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), and other diagnoses. Multivariable logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC), and classification and regression tree (CART) analyses were performed.

Results: Serum lactate differed significantly across diagnostic groups (P < 0.001) and was highest in patients with SZ and SAH. Among patients evaluated for ischemic stroke, age and serum lactate independently predicted SZ. ROC analysis showed moderate discrimination between SZ and ischemic stroke (INF/TIA) (area under the curve, 0.80; 95% confidence interval, 0.73-0.90). CART identified 4.05 mmol/L as the primary lactate threshold, with age providing additional stratification. Patients with lactate ≥4.05 mmol/L and age < 59.5 years had a 100% probability of SZ.

Conclusions: Serum lactate shows distinct distributions across neurologic emergencies encountered in the ED. Although not disease-specific, age-adjusted interpretation of serum lactate may improve seizure identification in patients presenting with suspected stroke. Because lactate measurement is rapid and routinely available, it may provide practical support for early diagnostic decision-making.

item.title: Activated partial thromboplastin time following Kcentra® versus Balfaxar® reversal of apixaban, rivaroxaban, and warfarin: a propensity-score matched cohort study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Kcentra® and Balfaxar® are the four-factor prothrombin concentrates (4F-PCCs) available in the United States. Both contain heparin to prevent in-vial activation, but Balfaxar® contains approximately 2-10 times more heparin versus Kcentra®. Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is commonly used to monitor heparin activity. This study compared aPTT changes following administration of Kcentra® versus Balfaxar® for apixaban, rivaroxaban, and warfarin reversal.

Methods: This single-center, retrospective, propensity-score matched cohort study included adults given Kcentra® or Balfaxar® for apixaban, rivaroxaban, or warfarin reversal. Patients had a baseline aPTT and a repeat aPTT within eight hours after 4F-PCC administration. Patients were matched 1:1 based on baseline aPTT and 4F-PCC dose. The primary outcome was aPTT change following administration. Secondary outcomes were hemostatic effectiveness within 24 h, new thrombotic events within seven days, and all-cause mortality within seven days.

Results: A total of 1026 orders were screened, of which 46 patients had a 4F-PCC order meeting inclusion criteria and 30 were successfully matched (15 in each group). Median (IQR) aPTT change was -1.2 (-5.4 to 0.9) s with Kcentra® and -2.4 (-10.7 to -0.4) s with Balfaxar®. The median difference (95% CI) was 2 (-3.2 to 9.1) s and was not statistically different between groups (p = 0.468). There was not a statistical difference between groups for hemostatic effectiveness, new thrombotic event, or all-cause mortality, but the CIs for the between-group differences were wide.

Conclusion: In this small propensity-score matched cohort of patients treated with apixaban, rivaroxaban, or warfarin, Kcentra® and Balfaxar® were not associated with significantly different changes in aPTT despite their markedly different heparin content. No statistically significant between-group differences were identified for hemostatic effectiveness, thrombotic events, or all-cause mortality, but the wide CIs preclude any conclusion of clinical equivalence. Larger studies focusing on patient-oriented outcomes are needed.

item.title: ED red blood cell transfusion in severe anemia: stay and recurrent use-a retrospective cohort study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion in the emergency department (ED) may occur during prolonged ED stays. We evaluated hospital stay and recurrent ED use among adults with severe anemia.

Methods: This retrospective cohort included ED encounters at a single tertiary academic hospital in Poland from January 2025-June 2026 with first hemoglobin <8.0 g/dL. Exposure was recorded ED RBC administration. Hospitalized encounters underwent propensity-score overlap weighting and patient-clustered bootstrap. Missing endpoints and available vital signs were recovered. Sensitivity analyses included 50 imputed datasets and weighted medians.

Results: Among 131,711 ED encounters, 1381 met eligibility criteria; 742 involved ED RBC transfusion. The hospitalized cohort included 610 encounters (175 with and 435 without ED RBCs). The adjusted total stay difference among survivors was 10.9 h (95% confidence interval [CI], -42.5 to 65.8); downstream estimates remained imprecise. ED stay was 9.4 h longer (95% CI, 8.0-10.8). Among 341 patients with transfusion followed by direct discharge, recurrent patients generated 52.1% of 541 episodes; 31.7% returned within 30 days.

Conclusions: Hospitalized encounters with recorded ED RBC administration had longer ED stays; treatment-related time could not be separated from waiting for inpatient beds. Downstream estimates allowed benefit or harm. Neither causal effects nor equivalence can be inferred. Pathways for stable recurrent anemia warrant evaluation while preserving urgent ED transfusion.

item.title: Co-administration of adrenaline and landiolol during cardiopulmonary resuscitation in a swine model of ventricular fibrillation
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Purpose: We examined whether early co-administration of landiolol and adrenaline improves successful extubation, hemodynamics, and 48-h outcomes in a swine ventricular fibrillation (VF) model.

Methods: In this prospective, randomized, investigator-blinded study, VF was electrically induced in healthy piglets and left untreated for 8 min. Thirty-nine female Landrace/Large White piglets were randomized (1:1:1): adrenaline 0.02 mg/kg plus saline, adrenaline plus esmolol 0.5 mg/kg, or adrenaline plus landiolol 0.02 mg/kg. Treatment was administered at the initiation of mechanical cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), 2 min before attempting defibrillation. Primary outcome was successful extubation. Secondary outcomes included return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), 48-h survival, 48-h survival with complete neurological recovery, and hemodynamic variables during and after CPR.

Results: Successful extubation occurred in 2/13 (15%) control, 6/13 (46%) esmolol, and 9/13 (69%) landiolol animals (overall p = 0.021); the rate was significantly higher with landiolol than with control (adjusted p = 0.046). ROSC rates were 46%, 69%, and 100%, respectively (p = 0.006); 48-h survival rates were 8%, 31%, and 54% (p = 0.046); and 48-h survival with complete neurological recovery rates were 0%, 23%, and 46% (p = 0.022). The landiolol group had higher observed rates of ROSC and 48-h survival with complete neurological recovery than the control group; these secondary analyses were exploratory. No pairwise difference was significant for 48-h survival. Exploratory analyses during the first 4 min of CPR identified higher observed values for selected hemodynamic variables and end-tidal carbon dioxide in the landiolol group at specific time points. Esmolol had intermediate observed outcome rates.

Conclusions: Early administration of landiolol with adrenaline was associated with a higher successful extubation rate and better observed early CPR hemodynamics compared with adrenaline alone and had the highest rates of ROSC, 48-h survival, and 48-h survival with complete neurological recovery. Secondary-outcome findings were exploratory, and landiolol was not statistically superior to esmolol.

item.title: Impact of an electronic health record visual cue on time to analgesia in patients with sickle cell in vaso-occlusive crisis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Management of painful vaso-occlusive crises (VOC), a hallmark of sickle cell disease (SCD), is a critical responsibility of emergency physicians (EPs). However, timely administration of opioid analgesia remains below the American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2020 guideline target.

Objectives: Our team implemented a technology-based intervention using a salmon-colored visual signal in the Electronic Health Record (EHR) to easily identify ED patients with SCD and prompt clinicians to prioritize patients with VOC. The study examined whether the intervention improved time to opioid administration for SCD VOC in a large urban academic ED.

Methods: This retrospective pre-post intervention study used EHR data for adult ED encounters with a diagnosis of SCD VOC over one year. The primary predictor was pre-intervention and post-intervention visits. Mixed-effects models examined associations between clinical outcomes and the primary predictor while accounting for repeated visits for VOC by the same patient. The primary outcome was mean time from ED arrival to first opioid administration. Secondary outcome was whether patients received the opioid within 60 min of ED arrival. A sensitivity analysis excluded high ED utilizers at various thresholds; more than 5, 10, 24, and 29 ED visits for SCD VOC.

Results: Among 841 ED encounters from 168 patients, mean time to first opioid was 66.3 min pre-intervention and 71.7 min post-intervention. Adjusted models indicated that time to first opioid administration was 2.50 min longer post-intervention (95% CI: -4.16 to 9.15). The odds of receiving first opioids within 60 min did not differ between intervention periods (aOR = 0.97, 95% CI: 0.71 to 1.32, absolute difference = 1.7, 95% CI: -5.1 to 8.4). Sensitivity analyses excluding high ED utilizers at four thresholds showed consistent results with primary analysis: 5-visit threshold (247 visits, adjusted difference = 3.4 min, 95% CI: -16.1 to 23); 10-visit threshold (377 visits, adjusted difference = 1.2 min, 95% CI: -11.6 to 14); 24-visit threshold (514 visits, adjusted difference = 4 min, 95% CI: -7.0 to 15.1); 29-visit threshold (572 visits, adjusted difference = 3.5 min, 95% CI: -6.4 to 13.3). None of these results reached statistical significance.

Conclusion: These findings suggest that passive EHR visual signals alone are insufficient to reduce analgesia delays in VOC, and that meaningful improvement will likely require multi-component, systems-based interventions integrating workflow redesign, nurse-initiated protocols, and automated clinical decision support.

Baughan AV, Okafor IM, Schechter-Perkins EM, Farrell NM, Leo MM, Nelson KP

item.title: Longer wait times after ED-initiated buprenorphine associated with lower appointment attendance
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Buprenorphine, a medication for opioid use disorder, improves patient outcomes, and emergency department induction of buprenorphine (EDIB) offers a low-barrier entry to treatment. While longer intervals between referral and first outpatient appointment in non-ED settings are known to decrease attendance, the effect of the interval between EDIB and first outpatient follow-up has not been established.

Objectives: To examine how the wait time between EDIB and the first outpatient appointment for medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) affects attendance at that initial visit. We tested the null hypothesis that wait time is not associated with attendance.

Methods: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, data were collected on adult ED patients who received EDIB (observed induction) or a buprenorphine prescription only (unobserved induction) between July 1, 2019, and December 31, 2025. Follow-up appointment attendance was obtained from referral centers. Chi-square, Fisher's exact, and Mann-Whitney U tests were used to compare attendance across demographic variables. Multivariable logistic regression estimated the adjusted odds ratio (AOR) of appointment attendance, controlling for demographics, insurance status, buprenorphine formulation, induction type, primary opioid, and polysubstance use. A Kaplan-Meier curve illustrated the relationship between appointment attendance and wait time.

Results: Of the 301 included individuals (65.4% male, 74.8% white, 30.9% insured), 51.2% attended the follow-up appointment. No associations were observed with demographics, substance use factors, or buprenorphine administration characteristics (all p > 0.05). Each additional day of wait time increased the odds of non-attendance by 31% (AOR = 1.310, 95% CI 1.099-1.560). The wait time at which attendance probability reached 50% was 3 days (95% CI 2.493-3.507).

Conclusions: A shorter wait time from EDIB to the first outpatient follow-up appointment is associated with increased appointment attendance. This study was limited to a single ED and may not be generalizable to all EDIB programs.

Jennings LK, Aven A, Lane S, Gainey S, Haynes L, Brady KT

item.title: Whole blood transfusion in adult patients with traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Whole blood (WB) transfusion may improve outcomes in trauma patients compared with component therapy, but evidence in traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains limited. We evaluated the clinical effectiveness of WB transfusion in adults with TBI requiring transfusion.

Methods: We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP for studies published from January 2006 through August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational studies using propensity score matching or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed for mortality. Component-specific transfusion requirements were summarized qualitatively.

Results: Five studies were included in the systematic review, and four studies were included in the mortality meta-analysis. WB transfusion was not clearly associated with lower mortality (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.62-1.16; P = 0.19; I2 = 48.3%), with a 95% prediction interval of 0.48-1.49. Sensitivity analyses using alternative effect-size conversion methods, baseline risks, effect measures, and mortality definitions yielded consistent results. In exploratory leave-one-out analyses, pooled RRs ranged from 0.74 to 0.91, with all 95% CIs including 1. Three studies contributed component-specific transfusion data; red blood cells and plasma requirements were generally lower with WB, although this may partly reflect substitution by WB itself. The certainty of evidence was very low.

Conclusions: Current evidence is insufficient to determine whether WB transfusion reduces mortality after TBI because of the limited number of studies, clinical and methodological heterogeneity, risk of bias, and imprecision. Further randomized trials in clearly defined TBI populations are needed.

Nagamura T, Taniguchi H, Utsumi S, Yamada K, Terayama T, Mukherjee K

item.title: Pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the emergency department: Factors associated with outcome
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Pediatric cardiac arrest is usually studied either before hospital arrival or after admission, although the emergency department (ED) team resuscitates both. We examined factors associated with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), recurrent arrest and mortality in an ED cohort including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA) and in-ED cardiac arrests.

Methods: Retrospective cohort of all 83 children who received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in a university pediatric ED over 14 years (January 2010-March 2024). The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge; multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with ED mortality.

Results: Median age was 35 months; 54.2% occurred out of hospital. ROSC was achieved in 42.2% and 30.1% survived the ED phase, but 9.9% survived to discharge. Epinephrine given later than 2 min was independently associated with ED mortality among the 27 patients with documented timing (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 7.73; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27-46.97). Beyond 20 min of CPR, each additional minute was associated with ED death (aOR 1.32; 95% CI 1.01-1.73). Recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED occurred in 42.9%, of whom 6.7% survived versus 38.9% without recurrence (p = 0.039). Survival did not differ by arrest location, initial rhythm or timing of advanced airway management.

Conclusion: Resuscitation in the ED restored spontaneous circulation in many children, but few survived to discharge. Time to first epinephrine was independently associated with ED mortality in this cohort, whereas prolonged resuscitation and recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED identified children at very high risk.

item.title: Modified pneumonia risk score using lung ultrasound for the prediction of radiographic pneumonia in children
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: The diagnosis of pneumonia in children based on clinical findings is challenging. The Pneumonia Risk Score (PRS), a clinical prediction tool, estimates the risk of radiographic pneumonia. Most children are classified as moderate-risk and are recommended to undergo chest x-ray (CXR). We hypothesized that lung ultrasound (LUS) may add diagnostic value beyond the PRS for predicting radiographic pneumonia.

Methods: We studied a convenience sample of children 6 months to 18 years old enrolled in a prospective LUS registry who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory complaints and underwent CXR and LUS. The primary outcome was radiographic pneumonia. Logistic regression included the five PRS clinical predictors, and LUS consolidation ≥1 cm with bronchograms was added to create the PRS + LUS model. We compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the PRS to the PRS + LUS, evaluated risk re-classifications, and proposed a novel diagnostic algorithm.

Results: Among 275 children, 58 (21%) had radiographic pneumonia. LUS consolidation was strongly associated with pneumonia (OR 28.68 [95% CI, 9.98 to 82.43]). The PRS + LUS demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy than the PRS alone (AUC 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.89] versus 0.70 [95% CI, 0.61 to 0.76]; P < 0.001). Using our proposed novel two-step diagnostic algorithm, the PRS + LUS was calculated for patients assigned a moderate-risk score by PRS, resulting in assigning an additional 120 (44%) patients a high- or low-risk score, decreasing the moderate-risk category.

Conclusion: Adding LUS to the PRS improves prediction of radiographic pneumonia and may reduce CXR use, particularly among patients with moderate risk.

Jarjour J, Neuman MI, Lipsett SC, Monuteaux MC, Hoffmann RM, Hirsch AW
